definition: Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery. CI automatically builds and tests every pushed commit; CD automatically ships builds that pass. The point is catching breakage minutes after it is introduced, not weeks later.
Test-Driven Development. Write a failing test first, write the minimum code to pass it, then refactor. The test defines 'done' before the code exists.
Object-Relational Mapper. A library (Prisma, Drizzle) that lets you query a SQL database through typed language objects instead of raw SQL strings.
Server-Side Rendering. HTML is generated on the server for each request and sent down ready to display, then JavaScript hydrates it to make it interactive.
Client-Side Rendering. The server sends a nearly empty HTML shell plus a JavaScript bundle; the browser builds the UI itself after the bundle loads.
Static Site Generation. Pages are rendered to HTML once at build time and served as static files — fastest possible delivery for content that rarely changes.
The process where client-side JavaScript attaches event listeners and state to server-rendered HTML, turning a static page into a live app. Mismatched server/client output causes hydration errors.
Cross-Origin Resource Sharing. A browser security policy: scripts on one origin cannot read responses from another origin unless the server opts in via Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers.

To change data in place. In REST it means any write operation (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE); in React it specifically refers to modifying state or props directly instead of producing a new object — which breaks re-rendering.
The actual data carried inside a request or response, as opposed to the headers and metadata wrapped around it.
Given the same inputs, the code always produces the same output. Deterministic functions are trivially testable; nondeterminism (random values, timestamps, network) is what makes tests flaky.
One authoritative place where a piece of state lives; everything else derives from it. Duplicating state in two places guarantees they will eventually disagree.
Document Object Model. The browser's live, in-memory tree representation of the page. JavaScript reads and mutates the DOM; the browser repaints to match.
Domain Name System. The distributed phone book that translates a human name (example.com) into an IP address the network can route to.
An operation that has the same effect whether run once or many times. PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not — a retried POST can create a duplicate.
A function that sits in the request pipeline between receiving a request and sending a response — auth checks, logging, body parsing. Each one can pass control onward or short-circuit.
Node's scheduling mechanism: one thread runs your JavaScript, while I/O waits elsewhere. Callbacks queue up and run when the stack is clear — which is why blocking the loop freezes everything.
React's diffing process: compare the new virtual tree against the previous one and apply the minimum set of real DOM mutations. Keys tell the diff which list items are 'the same' across renders.
A self-contained z-index universe created by properties like transform, opacity < 1, or position+z-index. A child can never escape its parent's stacking context, no matter how large its z-index.
A group of database statements that succeed or fail as one atomic unit. Either every statement commits, or the database rolls back to the state before any of them ran.
A versioned, replayable script that changes database schema (add a table, rename a column). Migrations let every environment evolve its schema identically.
A bug where the outcome depends on unpredictable timing between concurrent operations — e.g. two async responses arriving out of order and the stale one winning.
Caching a computation's result keyed by its inputs so repeat calls with the same inputs skip the work. React's useMemo/React.memo apply this to renders.
Representational State Transfer. An API style where URLs name resources (nouns) and HTTP methods express the action: GET reads, POST creates, PUT/PATCH updates, DELETE removes.
JSON Web Token. A signed, self-contained credential the server issues at login; the client sends it with each request so the server can verify identity without a session lookup.
A reverse API call: instead of you polling a service for changes, the service POSTs to a URL you registered whenever the event happens.
Delay running a handler until input has gone quiet for N milliseconds — e.g. fire a search request only after the user stops typing, not on every keystroke.
Passing data down through many component layers that don't use it, just so a deep child can. Context or state colocation are the usual cures.
